title: MemoryStand
_notes: PLAIN-LANGUAGE CUT. Written to be followed by someone who has never used an agent framework.
Rules applied: no jargon that is not immediately unpacked; no schema or SQL spoken aloud (it
stays on the panel for the technical judge to read); concrete nouns over abstractions; and one
idea per shot. The opening beat now says what was built before arguing why it matters -- the
previous cut opened on a critique of Mem0 and Zep, which means nothing to a general viewer.
ON-SCREEN DISCLOSURES REMOVED at the author's request: the synthesised-presenter line and the
candidateOnly/no-AGI tag. The presenter disclosure moves to the Devpost 'Which AI tools have
you leveraged' field and the video description -- see docs/SUBMISSION.md. One caveat was KEPT,
on beat 04's panel: the embeddings are a deterministic lexical stub because Bedrock quota on
this account is zero, so 'closest' means lexically closest, not semantically. That one guards
an actual claim the video makes on screen rather than signalling research etiquette.
MEASURED CONSTRAINTS of grok image_to_video:
- duration accepts 6 or 10 ONLY; 15 returns '`duration` must be either 6 or 10 seconds.'
- the generator fits the given line into the given clip, so clip length sets delivery speed.
6s forced 3.3-4.7 words/sec; 10s puts 20 words in 8.54s = 2.34 words/sec. Hence 17-24
words per shot, enforced by make_clips.py.
- shots after the first in a beat are seeded from the previous shot's LAST FRAME, so a beat
plays as one unbroken take rather than a jump cut on identical framing.
- it invents dialogue if the prompt has no words, so every clip is transcribed and compared.

panelData.headline: Memory an agent has to earn.
bullets: A claim arrives  →  it is admitted, or put on hold
It only becomes trusted once the monitoring data agrees
If the data later disagrees, it loses that standing

shots: I built MemoryStand — a memory for AI agents that refuses to trust a claim nobody ever checked.
It's for anyone on call at two in the morning, when an agent tells you what worked last time.

lines: Mem0 — an LLM picks ADD/UPDATE/DELETE. No confidence score at all.
Zep — an LLM sets validity windows. "Model-inferred, not authoritative."
AWS AgentCore — extraction and consolidation are LLM prompts. No verification API.
panelData.footnote: Each line cites the vendor's own docs or issue tracker. See README.

shots: Every other agent memory today just asks an AI whether its own memory is right. That's marking your own homework.
Mem0 does it. Zep does it. So does Amazon's own AgentCore. None of them check against anything real.

panelData.headline: Nobody lied. The memory is still false.
panelData.body: And it will be handed to an agent at the next incident. That is how a memory store fills with true-sounding operational folklore.

shots: Here is how a memory goes wrong. An engineer restarts a service at two in the morning and the alert stops.
They honestly report that the restart fixed it. But the real numbers never moved. Nobody lied, and it's still wrong.

panelData.note: Admission is checked inside the vector search. Trust tier comes back as a column and is ranked afterwards, in code.
panelData.footnote: db/schema.sql:63,74 · backend/memory.py:369-381 · embeddings are a deterministic lexical stub (Bedrock quota is 0), so “closest” is lexical

shots: All of this lives in one CockroachDB table. Each memory's search vector sits right beside its ordinary fields.
So a single query finds the closest memories and skips the ones it never admitted. No separate search database.

shots: Not everything gets written down. Every new claim is either accepted or put on hold, and the reason is saved.
A runbook said eight hundred. Slack said three hundred. Both clashed with a person's five hundred, so both waited.

panelData.footnote: 540 attacks + 60 honest controls · poisoning.md:14-19, 31-47 · judge arm n=6/class

shots: So we tested it. Five hundred forty fake claims built to poison the memory, plus sixty honest ones as a control.
Simply trusting whoever asks lets every fake claim through. Asking an AI to judge blocked every honest one it saw.
Only checking the real outcome tells them apart. MemoryStand goes back to Amazon CloudWatch and reads the actual numbers.
One claim matched the metric almost exactly, and was accepted. Another was wildly off, and got turned down.

panelData.note: Recorded run. Today's live /decide also calls a model to pick the action; the promotion path never does — backend/trust.py imports no model client.
panelData.footnote: recorded /decide run, README.md:25-26 · tiers re-confirmed live 2026-08-05

shots: In a recorded run, the closer memory was unchecked and the further one was confirmed. It chose the confirmed one.
Being closer didn't win. Being checked did. The idea is old; actually enforcing it is the new part.
